title: Going deeper in one
hook: some teachers say to go deep in one way rather than sampling forever

segments.voice: Yesterday, three warning signs: cut off, money pressed, questions forbidden. Your line was free to ask. Did you ask your honest question, and how was it received? Day one thousand four hundred seventeen.

"Everywhere means nowhere." Seneca wrote that in a letter to his friend Lucilius, warning him against reading one book, then another, then another, and settling into none. This path has been a tour, and tours are good. You've sat in a Zen hall and a Quaker meeting, counted the Omer, walked with the Stoics. But a tour can quietly turn into a habit of its own, always the next thing, never the same thing twice. Seneca's warning lands right here, near the end of the tour, with a question attached: at some point, do you stop visiting and start digging?
screen: `EVERYWHERE MEANS NOWHERE.` → `A TOUR CAN BECOME A HABIT.` → `STOP VISITING, START DIGGING?`

segments.voice: Seneca's letter makes the case with pictures. A traveler who is always on the road ends up with many acquaintances and no real friends. Food that leaves the stomach as soon as it's eaten never nourishes the body. A remedy changed every day never gets the chance to heal. His advice to Lucilius, in paraphrase, is to stay with a limited number of great writers and really digest them, rather than skimming everyone. Then he gives the line: "Everywhere means nowhere." Notice that Seneca isn't against reading widely. He reads other schools himself, and in the same letter he quotes Epicurus, whose school differed from his own. The point is depth, not narrowness. Some teachers in very different traditions say something similar about practice. Learn widely if you like, they say, but choose one way and stay with it long enough for it to change you, through the dull weeks and the dry months, past the part where it's new. A practice tried for a week shows you its surface. A practice kept for years starts to show you yourself. This isn't a call to change your faith, or to adopt one. If you already have a tradition, going deeper may simply mean returning to its own prayers, texts or practices with more attention. If you don't, it may mean choosing one practice from this tour, a sit, a walk, a nightly review, and keeping it. The image to hold is a well. Lots of shallow holes give you a damp field. One well, dug patiently, reaches water.
screen: `FRIENDS, NOT ACQUAINTANCES.` · `DEPTH, NOT NARROWNESS.` · `PAST THE PART WHERE IT'S NEW.` · `NOT A CALL TO CHANGE FAITHS.` · then, large: `ONE WELL REACHES WATER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one to deepen. Settle, and breathe. Let the practices you've met drift past: sitting, walking, singing, reading, reviewing the day, praying, if you pray. Don't choose the most exciting. Notice which one you keep returning to, or which one quietly helped. Let one stay, and let the others go by. Then picture keeping that one practice, the same way, at the same time, for a month. The bell holds the time.
Going deeper in one. Choosing one practice and staying with it past its newness, as Seneca advised staying with a few writers instead of skimming them all. Today's word.
Your line: one well, deep. Today, write down the one practice you chose and the time of day it lives in. Then do it once today, exactly as you will tomorrow. Day one thousand four hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: In some traditions, a practitioner settles into one main practice, such as a daily prayer, a sitting meditation or a regular study, and keeps it for years under a teacher or within a community, while still reading and learning more widely.

notes: Only 'Everywhere means nowhere.' is quoted from Gummere's Letter 2; the traveler, food, remedy and limited-writers images are paraphrased. Check the quote against a Gummere scan.
The script says Seneca 'quotes Epicurus' in the same letter; Letter 2 ends with a saying of Epicurus on poverty. Confirm.
The description of Lucilius as 'a restless reader' is hedged ('seems to have been'), inferred from the letter's advice. Confirm or cut.

The index hook says 'many teachers say'; under the claims rule the script says 'some teachers in very different traditions say something similar', naming none. The 'one well' image is presented as the path's own image, not attributed to any teacher.
The script states plainly that this is not a call to change or adopt a faith.
Editor pass: the hook no longer guesses that Lucilius 'seems to have been a restless reader'; it says what the letter does, warn against reading many books without settling.
